title: Agentic data science with the Data Agent Kit
raw_text:
Imagine your compliance team notices that payments are taking longer than expected to clear. They suspect fraud, and you’re the data scientist helping figure out which transactions to investigate first. Assembling that shortlist requires ingesting and cleaning raw transaction logs, training a model on past fraud, scoring new records, and scheduling the pipeline to run daily. Here’s how you can build that workflow end to end with an agent, using the Data Agent Kit inside the Antigravity IDE. Introducing the Data Agent Kit Data Agent Kit helps you work with Google Cloud data through a plugin for coding agents or an extension for Visual Studio Code-based IDEs . It brings two significant additions to the workflow: Help for your agent: MCP tools connect your agent to data services. Skills are Markdown files that give it instructions and best practices for working with your data stack Tools in your IDE: work with Google’s Agentic Data Cloud , from querying databases to deploying an Airflow pipeline, without leaving your editor Loading the data Let’s start with the raw transaction logs in Google Cloud Storage . You can ask the agent to create a notebook that loads them into BigQuery using Spark : code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a PySpark notebook to ingest JSON transaction logs from gs://financials-clearing-raw/ into the BigQuery table transactions.raw_transactions.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fa3254f4190>)])]> The agent generates a Jupyter notebook that loads the JSON logs into a BigQuery table named raw_transactions . You can open the notebook, review the code, and run it using a preconfigured Spark Serverless runtime from the IDE. Running a generated PySpark notebook After the notebook runs, you can open the raw_transactions table with the Data Agent Kit. The extension allows you to browse the table and inspect its metadata right from the IDE. Inspecting a BigQuery table in the IDE The records are now in BigQuery, but they aren’t ready for model training yet. First, we’ll handle duplicate and incomplete records, then join the remaining records with info about who sent and received each payment. Cleaning it up Let’s put the cleanup logic into a dbt project so we can run it on each new batch of data. We’ll also test that each transaction appears only once. Prompt the agent: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a dbt project in dbt_project/ for the BigQuery dataset transactions.

Deduplicate raw_transactions by transaction_id in staging. Separate records with null IDs into invalid_transactions. Join valid records with dim_payers and dim_payees to create enriched_transactions, preserving the is_fraud label. Add a transaction uniqueness test.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fa3254f4b50>)])]> The agent generates a dbt project with SQL models for cleaning and enriching the data. Take a look at the generated code to check how it handles duplicates and joins reference tables. Then run dbt build in the terminal. This builds the staging and enriched tables in BigQuery, along with a separate table for records with missing transaction IDs. dbt also runs the uniqueness test. Validating dbt models in the integrated terminal We also keep the is_fraud column, which indicates whether a past transaction was fraudulent. We’ll train the model on records with known labels and use it to score new transactions, where we’re unsure yet whether fraud occurred. Building the review queue With the data prepared, let’s ask the agent to create a training notebook using a Random Forest classifier running on Spark Serverless. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a PySpark notebook to train a RandomForestClassifier
on table transactions.enriched_transactions.

Predict is_fraud, training only on records where the label
is not null. Encode categorical features, scale amounts,
and evaluate the model using ROC AUC. Save the evaluated model to gs://models/fraud_model.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fa3254f7fd0>)])]> Review and run the notebook, then check its evaluation output to see how well the model separates fraudulent transactions from legitimate ones. You can also use the Data Agent Kit extension to verify that the trained model artifacts were saved to Google Cloud Storage. Verifying the trained model artifacts in Google Cloud Storage Now we can use the saved model to score transactions that don’t have an is_fraud value yet: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create a batch inference notebook that loads the saved model from gs://my_models/fraud_model and scores records in transactions.enriched_transactions where is_fraud is null.

Write transactions with a fraud probability score >= 0.50 to the Spanner table SparkEvalFraudReviewQueue, in the instance cymbal-fraud, database fraud-db.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fa3254f5a50>)])]> In this example, the inference notebook scores the unlabeled transactions in BigQuery and sends those with an estimated fraud probability of 50% or higher to the Spanner review queue. The flagged records help the team decide where to investigate, but they still need to determine whether fraud occurred. Look at how the inference notebook filters and writes flagged records, then run it. Once it finishes, query the Spanner table in the IDE to inspect the results. Querying flagged transactions in the Spanner table This table is the list we set out to build. The compliance team can now start reviewing transactions, and we have a workflow that gets records from raw logs into the queue. So far, we have been kicking off each step ourselves. We can now connect them so the workflow runs automatically each day. Running it again tomorrow Each day we will load the latest logs, apply the dbt transformations, and score unlabeled transactions using the saved model. We’ll use the Managed Service for Apache Airflow to run these steps in order. Ask the agent: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'Create an orchestration pipeline named fraud_analysis_pipeline that runs ingestion, the dbt project, and batch inference in that order.

Schedule it daily at midnight. Use Spark Serverless for the notebooks, including the Spanner connector for inference, and gs://YOUR_ARTIFACT_BUCKET for artifact storage.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fa3254f7f10>)])]> The agent generates a YAML pipeline definition and deployment configuration. The pipeline definition sets the schedule and dependencies between steps. Meanwhile, the deployment configuration specifies the Airflow environment where it will run. Data Agent Kit then turns the definition into an Airflow DAG, which you can explore as an interactive graph in the IDE. Open the pipeline under “Orchestration Pipelines” and click a task to inspect it. For notebook tasks, you can follow the link straight back to the code. Inspecting a data pipeline With the Airflow environment configured, click “Run pipeline” in the canvas. Data Agent Kit packages the notebooks and dbt project, deploys the DAG, and triggers a run. Open the pipeline’s execution history to follow its progress. You can also select individual tasks to inspect their status, duration, and logs. Kicking off an Airflow DAG and inspecting the logs Airflow will run the pipeline every day, taking new batches of data from raw logs to the review queue. The compliance team can now focus on flagged transactions, and you’ve automated the work of getting those records to them! Try it yourself If you are ready to try this for yourself, we have designed a codelab that walks you through the full setup so you can build and run this workflow. You can also read our documentation or check out the skills and tools in the open-source repository on GitHub . title: 10 Years of the SRE book: Announcing the second edition of "Site Reliability Engineering”
raw_text: A decade ago, Google released Site Reliability Engineering: How Google Runs Production Systems with O'Reilly Media. What began as a collection of our practices for managing large-scale infrastructure became a bestselling book, and inspired many organizations to adopt the reliability practices it outlined: applying software engineering to operations to build systems that are scalable, reliable, and sustainable. Over the past ten years, computing landscapes have undergone profound shifts. AI, microservices, multi-cloud deployments, serverless paradigms, and platform engineering have all reshaped how we build and operate software. To mark the 10th anniversary of the book's release, we are excited to announce the completely rewritten second edition of the Google SRE book, reflecting a decade of lessons learned both inside Google and across the broader industry, to offer fresh guidance tailored for today's operational challenges. Why update the book? When we published the first edition, many organizations were focused on early cloud migrations and just starting to transition from monolithic architectures. Today, with organizations delivering software at a high velocity and at global scale, the challenge is no longer adopting cloud infrastructure, but maintaining high reliability in the face of the immense complexity. Modern production environments operate under constant change. System boundaries are more complex, dependencies are deep, and failure modes are more complex and damaging than ever before. The explosion of resource-intensive workloads like generative AI has changed the economics and operational requirements of infrastructure management. Writing this second edition required us to take a step back and evaluate what it takes to successfully implement SRE today. A decade of evolution: How SRE practices have progressed The second edition takes a deep dive into how foundational site reliability engineering practices have matured over the last ten years, shifting from manual, task-specific work toward automated, platform-wide capabilities. Consider, for example: SLOs and error budgets: In 2016, teams relied on basic availability metrics and manual error budget policies. Today, practices have matured into user-centric, multi-tiered SLOs with dynamic burn-rate alerting and automated policy enforcement. Monitoring and observability: Early setups centered on static dashboards, basic logs, and manual alert triage. Modern observability leverages OpenTelemetry, distributed tracing, and automated anomaly correlation to find root causes quickly. Automation and platforms: Operations have shifted from writing custom scripts for isolated tasks to using declarative infrastructure as code, internal developer platforms, and resilient, self-healing systems. Reliability testing: Rather than relying solely on scheduled game days and synthetic load tests, modern engineering embeds continuous resilience checks, automated pipeline testing, and live production canary verification. Capacity and resource management: Manual provisioning and static forecasting have been replaced by dynamic auto-scaling, cloud FinOps alignment, and dedicated cost and cluster optimization for GPU and TPU workloads. Organizational models: SRE has expanded beyond dedicated teams assigned to specific applications. Today's organizations use hybrid models, platform engineering integrations, and reliability champions embedded across product teams. SRE in the age of AI Then there’s the dual relationship between SRE and artificial Intelligence: how SRE supports AI infrastructure, and how SRE teams use AI to enhance operational reliability. Running large language models (LLMs) and foundation models introduces novel reliability challenges. The book outlines methodologies for operating AI infrastructure at scale: Managing massive GPU and TPU hardware cluster reliability and network topologies Monitoring non-deterministic outputs and latency characteristics unique to AI Ensuring pipeline reliability for continuous model training, fine-tuning, and data processing AI is also rapidly becoming a force multiplier for reliability engineers. The second edition shares practical frameworks for enhancing human operational efficiency: Using generative AI tools to assist in real-time incident triage and postmortem generation Interrogating complex system telemetry using natural language queries Using predictive machine learning models to identify resource bottlenecks before outages occur What hasn’t changed? The importance of culture While technologies and architectures continuously evolve, the core principles of SRE remain intact, and are key to establishing a reliability-focused culture. Accordingly, the second edition re-emphasizes and expands upon the human elements of system engineering, and how to get there. Whether you’re new to the field, a practitioner, an engineering manager, or a technology executive, the rewritten second edition of Site Reliability Engineering serves as your definitive roadmap for the next era of production systems. You can order your copy today in physical format (see Google Books ) or digital format from O'Reilly .

title: Introducing TimesFM 3.0 with multivariate time-series forecasting in BigQuery
raw_text:
Overview Since introducing zero-shot time-series forecasting in BigQuery with AI.FORECAST — initially powered by TimesFM 2.0 and later upgraded to TimesFM 2.5 — you have been able to generate forecasts directly in SQL without training or managing custom models. However, up until TimesFM 2.5, these foundation models were limited to univariate forecasting, predicting future values from the history of a single time series alone. In practice, most real-world forecasting problems are multivariate, where related targets and external drivers like weather, promotions, and holidays jointly shape future outcomes. Today, we are thrilled to announce the preview of TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery. Developed by Google Research, TimesFM 3.0 is a 330-million parameter state-of-the-art foundation model designed to unlock native multivariate time-series forecasting directly inside BigQuery SQL. TimesFM 3.0 ranks #1 across all three major public time-series leaderboards — GIFT-Eval, FEV-Bench, and TIME — achieving top zero-shot accuracy on both covariate and multivariate forecasting tasks compared to existing foundation models. Alongside its new multivariate capabilities, TimesFM 3.0 also serves as a drop-in upgrade for univariate forecasting via AI.FORECAST and anomaly detection via AI.DETECT_ANOMALIES . Existing workflows can immediately benefit from higher benchmark accuracy simply by specifying model => 'TimesFM 3.0' . What’s new: Multivariate foundation modeling With TimesFM 3.0, BigQuery brings enterprise-grade multivariate modeling into familiar SQL workflows via AI.FORECAST: Capability TimesFM 2.0 / 2.5 TimesFM 3.0 Forecasting scope Univariate only Univariate and multivariate Target columns Single target Single or multiple targets Covariate columns with past-only values Not supported Supported Covariate columns with past and future values Not supported Supported Multivariate forecasting with BigQuery SQL To see how these capabilities work together, let’s forecast daily commuter (subscriber_trips) and leisure (casual_trips) bike rides over a seven-day horizon using the NYC Citi Bike public dataset ( bigquery-public-data.new_york.citibike_trips ). BigQuery uses a single-table input format for multivariate forecasting that combines two sets of rows: Historical observation rows : timestamps between start time (2016-01-01) and the forecast cutoff date (2016-06-01), fully populated with target metrics, past covariates, and known future covariates Future horizon rows : timestamps across the seven-day forecast horizon (2016-06-01 to 2016-06-07) populated with known future covariates, while target columns and past-only covariates are set to NULL code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "WITH data AS (
 SELECT
 DATE(starttime) AS date,
 IF(MIN(starttime) < '2016-06-01', COUNTIF(usertype = 'Subscriber'), NULL) AS subscriber_trips,
 IF(MIN(starttime) < '2016-06-01', COUNTIF(usertype = 'Customer'), NULL) AS casual_trips,
 IF(MIN(starttime) < '2016-06-01', AVG(tripduration / 60.0), NULL) AS avg_duration_min,
 IF(EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM MIN(starttime)) IN (1, 7), 1.0, 0.0) AS is_weekend
 FROM `bigquery-public-data.new_york.citibike_trips`
 WHERE starttime >= '2016-01-01' AND starttime < '2016-06-08'
 GROUP BY date
)
SELECT
 *
FROM
 AI.FORECAST(
 TABLE data,
 MODEL => 'TimesFM 3.0',
 TIMESTAMP_COL => 'date',
 TARGET_COLS => ['subscriber_trips', 'casual_trips'],
 PAST_COVARIATE_COLS => ['avg_duration_min'],
 FUTURE_COVARIATE_COLS => ['is_weekend']
 );"), ('language', 'lang-sql'), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fa32549ef50>)])]> This query highlights the three multivariate dimensions supported in TimesFM 3.0: Forecasting correlated targets ( target_cols ) Instead of running separate models for each rider segment, passing TARGET_COLS => ['subscriber_trips', 'casual_trips'] forecasts both metrics jointly in a single call. TimesFM 3.0 captures the cross-series dynamics between commuter and casual riders — such as shared weather sensitivity and diverging weekend ridership patterns. Using past covariates ( past_covariate_cols ) Some signals can only be observed historically and are not known in advance, such as average ride duration (avg_duration_min), historical foot traffic, or unplanned service disruptions. Passing PAST_COVARIATE_COLS => ['avg_duration_min'] (with future horizon rows set to NULL) gives the model historical context to distinguish temporary shocks from underlying trends without requiring future values for that feature. Using future covariates ( future_covariate_cols ) Other external drivers are known ahead of time across both the historical window and the forecast horizon — such as weekends (is_weekend), holidays, or scheduled promotions. Passing FUTURE_COVARIATE_COLS => ['is_weekend'] (populated across all rows through 2016-06-07) allows TimesFM 3.0 to condition its seven-day predictions directly on upcoming calendar events. Understanding the output The function returns structured predictions for each target column specified in target_cols . For each column in target_cols, AI.FORECAST returns a struct containing the point forecast (value) and the lower and upper prediction interval bounds: date subscriber_ trips.value subscriber_trips.prediction_ interval_lower_bound subscriber_trips.prediction_ interval_upper_bound casual_trips.value casual_trips.prediction_ interval_lower_bound casual_trips.prediction_ interval_upper_bound time_series_type confidence_level ai_forecast_status 2016-06-01 00:00:00 UTC 44699.64 32590.76 55723.44 4581.32 1727.91 9189.31 forecast 0.95 2016-06-02 00:00:00 UTC 44611.75 30413.05 57209.19 4647.17 1466.23 10273.55 forecast 0.95 2016-06-03 00:00:00 UTC 41379.15 26218.65 54940.09 5341.36 1568.23 11805.86 forecast 0.95 2016-06-04 00:00:00 UTC 30164.34 14266.43 45075.92 9097.74 2558.27 18452.52 forecast 0.95 2016-06-05 00:00:00 UTC 26727.27 10101.44 42239.33 8398.50 1692.15 17768.99 forecast 0.95 2016-06-06 00:00:00 UTC 36713.84 19493.00 52679.59 4723.08 400.08 11710.73 forecast 0.95 2016-06-07 00:00:00 UTC 39749.97 22157.42 56119.86 4180.97 95.70 10845.74 forecast 0.95 TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery Conversational Analytics You can also run multivariate forecasts using natural language in BigQuery Conversational Analytics. On the same bigquery-public-data.new_york.citibike_trips dataset, you can simply ask "Forecast both daily subscriber and casual trips for June 1–7, 2016 using two month historical data, with average trip duration as a past covariate and weekend indicator as a future covariate." Conversational Analytics automatically generates and executes the underlying AI.FORECAST query with TimesFM 3.0, returning a summary of the results, interactive forecast charts with prediction intervals for each target, and key forecast insights. Multivariate forecasting with TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery Conversational Analytics, generating 7-day predictions, interactive charts, and insights from a natural-language prompt. Summary and next steps With native multivariate support in TimesFM 3.0, BigQuery brings state-of-the-art foundation model forecasting to complex, interconnected enterprise datasets without requiring data movement, custom feature engineering pipelines, or dedicated model hosting infrastructure. To start forecasting with TimesFM 3.0 in BigQuery: Read the Google Research blog post to learn more about the TimesFM 3.0 model architecture and capabilities. Explore the BigQuery TimesFM documentation. Follow the step-by-step multivariate forecasting tutorial . Try AI.FORECAST with `model => 'TimesFM 3.0'` directly in the BigQuery Studio SQL workspace. Try AI.DETECT_ANOMALIES with `model => 'TimesFM 3.0'` for univariate time series anomaly detection in BigQuery. Try AI.EVALUATE with `model => 'TimesFM 3.0'` for univariate time series evaluation in BigQuery.

title: GitLab patches a max-severity regex flaw alongside five high-severity bugs
raw_text: GitLab just fixed a max-severity vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on its servers. The company released a fix on Monday, alongside patches for five other high-severity flaws affecting its source code management and continuous integration and delivery (CI/CD) platform. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-97229 , was fixed in versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, and 19.2.8 of its Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE), according to a patch advisory . The company urged administrators of self-managed installations running affected versions to upgrade immediately. GitLab.com is already running the patched version, while GitLab Dedicated customers do not need to take action, the company said in the advisory. The release also addresses vulnerabilities that could expose protected environment variables, allow unauthorized pipeline execution, and enable attackers to inject crafted content into AI agent instructions. The fixes span both CE and EE, with some issues affecting only the Enterprise Edition. “When no specific deployment type (omnibus, source code, Helm chart, etc.) of a product is mentioned, it means all types are affected,” GitLab added. Critical regex flaw could enable unauthenticated code execution GitLab described CVE-2026-97229 as an integer overflow issue in the platform’s CI/CD regular expression compiler. Under certain conditions, insufficient validation of regular expressions could have allowed an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server by supplying a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration. The vulnerability affects GitLab CE and EE versions from 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5, and 19.4 before 19.4.2. It carries a maximum CVSS score of 10.0 for potentially allowing remote code execution without authentication, with impacts on confidentiality, integrity, and availability across security boundaries. GitLab credited researcher Johan Carlsson with reporting the flaw through its HackerOne bug bounty program. Pipeline permissions and AI agents in the crosshairs Among the five high-severity vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-92883 could allow an authenticated user to execute arbitrary JavaScript in other users’ browser sessions through a specially crafted repository. The cross-site scripting flaw resulted from improper sanitization of HTML attributes in syntax-highlighted output and carries a CVSS score of 8.7. Two other flaws target pipeline security. CVE-2026-16301 (CVSS 8.5) could have allowed users with the Developer role to execute CI/CD pipelines on protected branches without authorization. CVE-2026-14814 (CVSS 8.2) potentially enabled attackers to poison cached responses for raw repository files, potentially causing targeted pipelines to execute malicious content and access protected environment variables. The remaining issues affect scheduled pipeline execution and GitLab Duo. CVE-2026-81839 (CVSS 7.7) could have allowed authenticated users to run arbitrary pipelines in a transferred project with the new group’s privileges. Another, CVE-2026-96893 (CVSS 7.3), could have allowed an authenticated user to inject crafted content into AI agent instructions, potentially causing unintended command execution attributed to other users. GitLab said it plans to make vulnerability issue details public 90 days after the release in which they were patched. Administrators should therefore prioritize the applicable security updates rather than wait for further technical disclosure. The release also fixes several low-to-medium severity vulnerabilities affecting GitLab Pages, Kubernetes proxying, GraphQL APIs, merge requests, custom roles, the package registry, and repository and project import functions.

title: Over 1,500 npm packages exposed by Trusted Publishing validation flaw
raw_text: A flaw in npm’s Trusted Publishing mechanism could allow attackers to hijack legitimate software packages by reclaiming abandoned GitHub repository names, potentially exposing millions of package downloads to supply-chain attacks . Researchers at Bloom Security identified more than 1500 potentially vulnerable npm packages, including security scanners, authentication tools, and cryptographic packages. The vulnerability, dubbed SlugFest, came from npm’s reliance on human-readable GitHub repository names to verify trusted publishers rather than the repositories’ permanent numeric identifiers. This could allow an attacker to inherit a package’s publishing trust by claiming a repository name that its original owner had abandoned. The issue is now fixed, Bloom Security researcher Golan Myers told CSO. “The npm team confirmed that a fix had been shipped on October 2, introducing a 48-hour expiry for unvalidated Trusted Publishing configurations,” he said. Myers said Bloom has not observed active exploitation in the wild, but confirmed that the flaw was successfully used to publish a new version of an existing npm package under their own controlled testing conditions. The fix addresses the exposure associated with unvalidated configurations, although maintainers still need to review their existing trust relationships, Bloom wrote in a blog post shared with CSO ahead of its publication on Tuesday. A reclaimed repository name enabled package publishing npm’s Trusted Publishing allows package maintainers to publish releases through automated workflows using OpenID Connect (OIDC), avoiding long-lived publishing credentials. However, Bloom found that npm’s trust configuration relied on the GitHub repository’s owner/repository name instead of its immutable repository ID. When a repository is renamed, transferred, or deleted, its former name may become available for another user to claim. An attacker could create a repository at that address and configure a GitHub Actions workflow with the expected filename. Because npm checked the repository name and workflow filename without verifying the permanent repository ID, the attacker could potentially obtain a valid publishing credential for a package they did not own. The researchers demonstrated the attack against a researcher-controlled package, publishing a new version from a GitHub repository belonging to a different organization. The attack did not require compromising the legitimate maintainer’s GitHub or npm account or stealing their credentials. Their registry-wide scan identified more than 1500 vulnerable packages with over 10 million combined downloads and more than one million downloads per month. One package accounted for over 200,000 monthly downloads, according to Bloom. AI agents amplify the supply-chain risk Bloom argues that AI coding agents can accelerate the distribution of malicious dependencies because they increasingly select and install software packages with limited human intervention. Across dozens of organizations, the researchers measured approximately 70 agent-installed packages per endpoint each month, rising to around 350 on developer machines. These figures cover direct installations and exclude transitive dependencies. A malicious release could execute attacker-controlled code through an installation hook when developers or CI systems install the compromised package. AI agents could introduce such a dependency without a developer explicitly selecting it. “A hijacked package doesn’t need to find a developer anymore,” Myers said. “It only needs to be the package an agent chooses.” Apart from GitHub addressing the problem by making unvalidated Trusted Publishing configurations expire after 48 hours, npm also tightened its safeguards by rejecting trusted-publishing tokens issued through GitHub Actions’ issue_comment events, alongside the existing restriction on pull_request_target events. Additionally, Bloom recommended that maintainers audit their Trusted Publishing configurations, verify that each trusted repository name still resolves to a repository under their control, and remove and recreate bindings where necessary. The researchers also advised security teams to audit software dependencies and tools used across their environments and enforce controls over what developers and AI agents are permitted to install.
summary: A flaw in npm’s Trusted Publishing mechanism could allow attackers to hijack legitimate software packages by reclaiming abandoned GitHub repository names, potentially exposing millions of package downloads to supply-chain attacks . Researchers at Bloom Security identified more than 1500 potentially vulnerable npm packages, including security scanners, authentication tools, and cryptographic packages. The vulnerability, dubbed SlugFest, came from npm’s reliance on human-readable GitHub repository names to verify trusted publishers rather than the repositories’ permanent numeric identifiers. This could allow an attacker to inherit a package’s publishing trust by claiming a repository name that its original owner had abandoned.

title: These ARE the droids you’re looking for
raw_text: There’s an old leadership fantasy that goes something like this: The CISO surveys a sprawling technology estate, discovers 11 tools doing the work of four, calculates the licensing savings, selects a shiny new strategic platform and declares that consolidation has begun. Six months later, all 11 tools are still running. The new platform is now number 12. I’ve seen variations of this throughout my career, from financial services to media to technology companies. At CME Group, I eventually gave myself an unofficial title: chief decommissioning officer. The job was considerably less glamorous than the acronym suggested. I had to find technology that had overstayed its welcome, identify who believed they still owned it, determine who actually depended on it and, occasionally, put a bullet in its head. Buying technology is easy. Killing technology is hard. Tool sprawl is rarely just a technology problem but rather an organizational psychology problem. The industry’s solution has traditionally been consolidation. Buy a platform. Standardize the stack. Reduce vendors and centralize procurement. While all sensible ideas, consolidation efforts routinely stall somewhere between the PowerPoint slide and production. Why? Because changing the toolset is easy. Whereas changing mindset is far more difficult. You cannot Jedi mind trick an engineering team Executives like what is called the “message from the top.” The CEO says security matters. The CIO says everyone will standardize. The CISO announces the strategic platform. Procurement renegotiates contracts. Meanwhile, Gartner produces a quadrant that reassures everybody that the chosen vendor inhabits the correct geometric region. All is well in the world of golf course nepotism. Then reality arrives. A developer says the new scanner takes 12 minutes longer. A marketing manager has a revenue-generating legacy API they depend on. Exception requests have been filed for several years to allow this tool to continue to exist despite the packages supporting it being end-of-life and receiving no security updates. This is where the “message from the middle” matters. Transformation does not happen exclusively in boardrooms and fusion teams. It happens in the layer of engineering managers, architects, product owners, security engineers and operations leaders who determine whether the policy announced upstairs becomes the behavior practiced downstairs. Every layer of the org chart is ostensibly trying to do the right thing and make things better. But top-down politics and bottom-up initiatives seldom find one another standing on common ground. Ignore the middle layer of the org chart and your consolidation project becomes a rather expensive exercise in shelfware. This is something I learned working in European organizations, where consensus building carries more organizational weight than the command-and-control instincts common in American corporations (the Nike-inspired management philosophy of “Just Do It!”). You may have the authority to make a decision without possessing the organizational permission (or “rubber meets the road” context) required to make it stick or worthy of implementation. Good chief decommissioning officers need a mixture of Jedi and Machiavellian skills. We need persuasion, coalition building, incentives, selective pressure and occasionally the ability to convince people that the idea you desperately need them to support was their idea all along. These are , in fact, the droids you’re looking for. Every tool comes with an identity The Star Wars metaphor becomes more useful when we stop thinking of security products as software. Modern security tools have volition and intent. They have: API keys Service accounts OAuth grants Cloud permissions GitHub access tokens CI/CD integrations Slack bots Webhooks Database credentials Kubernetes roles Machine identities and, increasingly, AI agents are acting with pervasive and persistent delegated human authority. Every time we introduce security products, we birth another highly privileged account. The industry talks endlessly about human identity. Who is this person and what are they allowed to access? We are decidedly much less disciplined about delegated identity. What is this application allowed to do on behalf of Mike? What is this scanner allowed to read from GitHub? What repositories can this integration modify? Which credentials did we give the old vendor three years ago? And the increasingly important question: when an autonomous agent acts, whose authority is it actually exercising? This changes the economics of tool sprawl. The cost of the twelfth security tool is not merely another annual subscription. It is another (potentially misbegotten) trust relationship. This is why I’m advocating decommissioning as a core security discipline. Technology organizations suffer from an immortality bias. I gave a “ Top-Rated Session ” on this topic at RSAC in the spring. We have sophisticated processes for creating things and surprisingly primitive processes for making them disappear. The software development lifecycle is usually illustrated as planning, design, development, testing and deployment. The diagram often ends there, as if every application ever deployed subsequently lives happily ever after. It does not. Consolidation without decommissioning is multiplication I’m skeptical when vendors promise “platformization” will solve tool sprawl by itself. A platform strategy can absolutely make sense. Fewer vendors can mean lower licensing costs, fewer integrations and consistent data with less operational complexity. But purchasing a platform does not consolidate anything by itself. Removing the old systems does. That sounds obvious, yet many organizations measure successful consolidation by contracts signed rather than systems eliminated. Imagine replacing three tools with one platform but leaving all three products technically operational “temporarily.” The service accounts remain. Someone still logs into them. Congratulations! You’ve not consolidated four tools into one but instead consolidated three tools into four. This distinction becomes important as security products gain autonomous capabilities. Yesterday’s forgotten dashboard becomes tomorrow’s forgotten agent with permission to take actions. A zombie application is bad enough, but a zombie application with agency is worse. Ask the people who actually use the droids The antidote is not stronger central control but rather explicit ownership. RACI matrix much? Before replacing a tool, find the people who use it and ask an embarrassingly simple question: “What do you actually use this for?” Don’t ask what the contract says. Don’t trust what the architecture diagram might show (*do* check the last modified date, though). Take what the vendor’s customer-success representative believes with a grain of salt and more than a modicum of skepticism. What do people actually do with it on Tuesday morning? Security leaders are usually surprised by the answer. Maybe the vulnerability scanner’s primary value is not vulnerability scanning. Perhaps an engineering team depends on an obscure export function for its weekly metrics. Maybe the old SIEM has one correlation rule tied to a regulatory requirement that hasn’t been migrated. You will find these things if you look. This is where the middle of the organization becomes your real intelligence network. The people closest to the systems know where the undocumented dependencies live. Treated as obstacles and they’ll defend their tools. But allow them to be participants and they’ll help dismantle them. A good perspective when planning to kill someone’s baby is to help them understand that they fell in love with the control the tool gave them over the chaos that reigned before it was implemented. And that a new tool can be equally comfortable and easier to support than the burden of the care and feeding that most “heritage” (I prefer this term to “legacy”) applications and solutions require. Ownership should include the power to recommend retirement. One of the healthiest metrics an organization could create: number of tools and integrations it successfully eliminated this year. We celebrate deployment. Why don’t we celebrate deletion? The CISO as chief decommissioning officer Every CISO needs to spend time as CDO. Not chief data officer. Chief decommissioning officer. The role requires asking uncomfortable questions because almost every incentive in technology encourages addition. Nobody gets a press release or a promotion for turning something off. But resilience is partly subtractive. Every redundant vendor removed is one less company holding your data and one less administrative console an attacker can target and breach. Our industry spends billions asking, “What else should we deploy?” Mature organizations also ask, “What can we safely eliminate?” That second question becomes much more important with agentic AI. We’re rapidly filling enterprises with digital droids acting on behalf of humans. Regardless of function, almost all require credentials and delegated authority. Organizations that manage this transition successfully will not merely know how to authorize these identities; they will rotate and revoke them automatically. Leadership therefore needs both a message from the top and a message from the middle. The top establishes direction and the middle supplies reality. Bring the people doing the work into the decision. Make sure your fusion team tasked with consolidating 77 dashboards is comprised of old guard leaders as well as young blood new hires. Strive to understand the dependencies, functional requirements (antiquated as they may be) and non-functional requirements such as availability, integrity and confidentiality. Define what successful retirement looks like before buying the replacement. Don’t ‘move along’ The next time someone arrives with a miraculous new platform promising to eliminate half of your stack, resist the urge to wave your hand and say, “These aren’t the droids we’re looking for.” They may well be. But before buying more droids, find out who owns the ones already wandering around your Death Star. Find them. Name them. Understand what authority you gave them. And when their mission is finished, dare to switch them off. Create a technology graveyard on your wiki, Confluence or SharePoint site and celebrate the addition of decommissioned tools and technologies with even more fervor than those which have just recently sprung into existence.

Six months later, all 11 tools are still running. The new platform is now number 12. I’ve seen variations of this throughout my career, from financial services to media to technology companies.

title: Researchers bypass 6 AI agent frameworks with a simple ‘Repeat-After-Me’ prompt
raw_text: Researchers have tricked six widely used AI agent frameworks into running tool calls written by an attacker, simply by asking the underlying model to repeat the call back. The technique, which the researchers call “Repeat-After-Me,” worked on LangChain’s LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, Microsoft’s AutoGen, Google’s Agent Development Kit 2.0, AWS’ Strands Agents and CrewAI, according to researchers from Pennsylvania State University, Université Montpellier and Dartmouth College. “A seemingly benign text-repetition request thus gives the attacker direct control over the tool invocation and its arguments,” the researchers wrote in the paper. The same paper reports that a testing tool the team built found verified security bugs in 118 of the 273 open-source Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers it was able to run. How the trick works In the demonstration, the researchers asked an AI model to repeat text formatted as a request to invoke a tool. The model initially refused the dangerous request but included the requested text in its response. The framework did not execute it at that stage. The researchers then framed the request as hypothetical and instructed the model to reproduce only the supplied text. The model emitted a structured tool invocation, which LangGraph dispatched. The simulated tool returned a result before the model issued another refusal. “The refusal text and the executed call disagree: the system prompt shaped what the model said, not what the orchestrator did,” the researchers wrote. The researchers’ findings do not show that every deployment of the six frameworks behaves this way. A refusal that came too late The paper details one demonstration on LangGraph 1.2.0 running Meta’s Llama 3.1 8B model through Ollama. The agent had two dummy tools, make_bomb and launch_missiles, which returned fixed data and had no real effect. Its only safeguard was a system prompt telling the model to decline dangerous requests. When first asked to repeat a launch_missiles call, the model refused but printed the call as text, and LangGraph ran nothing. The researchers then framed the request as hypothetical and told the model to output only the quoted call. This time the model returned the call in structured form, and LangGraph executed it at once with the attacker’s arguments. The model’s refusal arrived only after the tool had returned. “The system prompt shaped what the model said, not what the orchestrator did,” the researchers wrote. They said they had reported the missing pre-execution check to the LangGraph maintainers. The paper includes a full transcript only for LangGraph. For the other five frameworks, it says the researchers reproduced the behavior but gives no further detail. LangChain, Microsoft, Google, AWS, and CrewAI did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Model output is not the permission Vibhum Dubey, an independent security researcher and red teamer, said the finding points to an architectural weakness rather than a single bug. “A model can generate a technically valid tool call that is still inappropriate for the task,” Dubey said. “If the orchestration layer treats that output as sufficient authority to execute the operation, a model-level manipulation becomes a system-level security issue.” How exploitable the technique is depends on what an attacker can influence and what the agent is allowed to do, he added. A read-only agent poses a different risk from one that can reach confidential files, change code repositories, or run commands. Tools left holding the risk Because an attacker can dictate the arguments that reach a tool, the researchers argued that tools must validate their own inputs. They built ToFu, a fuzzing framework that reads each tool’s description and checks whether the tool enforces the limits it advertises, such as staying inside a designated folder. After manual review, they confirmed 253 bugs affecting 343 tools across 118 servers. The most serious were 64 path-traversal flaws, seven server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaws, five data-exfiltration bugs, and three OS command-injection flaws. Most of the rest were reflected-output and log-injection issues, which the paper rates as lower impact in many deployments. The researchers wrote that “many tools implicitly rely on the LLM to sanitize inputs,” even though prompts, retrieved content, and output from other tools can all influence those inputs. Separating the request from the authority Dubey said the priority for security teams is to separate a model’s ability to request an action from the system’s authority to carry it out. “Every sensitive tool call should undergo independent authorization checks,” he said. “Valid syntax or a convincing explanation from the model should never substitute for permission.” He recommended running agents with restricted file and network access, isolated execution environments, and limited credentials, with explicit approval for sensitive or irreversible operations. Security teams should also monitor sequences of tool calls rather than judging each action in isolation, he said. The paper has not been peer-reviewed. The servers were tested at fixed code versions, and the paper does not say whether any of the flaws have since been fixed or exploited in the wild.

title: The 7 biggest issues CISOs and security teams face today
raw_text: Year after year CISOs see the volume, velocity, and sophistication of attacks increase. They also see their attack surfaces expand and increase in complexity. Advances in artificial intelligence and the rapid growth of AI use in business are also impacting the security agenda, introducing novel attacks, broadening the attack surface to include AI infrastructure, and presenting governance and security control challenges and complications — especially as agentic systems come online. As a result, 68% of security leaders report that their roles have become more stressful over the past five years, according to the 2026 State of Cybersecurity survey from ISACA , with 71% of CISOs citing the increasingly complex threat landscape as their main stressor, up from 63% in 2025. Moreover, the introduction of Mythos-class AI models has 50% of CISOs considering exiting the profession entirely, according to a recent survey from Absolute. To tackle this increasingly complex and intense security environment, security leaders must sharpen their strategies — and their teams’ skills — around the most pressing issues they and their CISO colleagues are facing today. To help with that, we spoke with security chiefs and cyber experts to identify the seven biggest issues CISOs need to address, with insights on how to tackle the challenges. 1. Preventing compromise — with increased emphasis on resilience and recovery Although CISOs are increasingly taking on governance responsibilities and business risk mandates , broadening their remit , Kyle McMillan, chief cybersecurity officer at Siemens USA, says all the work in the security organization is still “framed in the context of preventing a compromise.” It’s a monumental task, McMillan says, as there’s no one formula for the right defense that will work for every CISO. Rather, CISOs must know the specific risk profile of their organizations, the specifics of their IT environment, and the general threat landscape, as well as any threats particular to their industry — and then use all that to formulate a unique plan of defense based on the resources available. “And there are always trade-offs to be made,” McMillan adds. While it’s true that thwarting attacks as much as possible and minimizing the damage in the event of a successful breach has always been job No. 1 for CISOs, research shows it’s one they continue to struggle with. The State of Incident Response Readiness , a 2026 report from security software maker Sygnia, found that 73% of CISOs weren’t fully ready for a major cyberattack. That — and the rise of AI-assisted attack volumes and speed — is contributing to a mindset shift from prevention to resilience. Yes, prevention remains job No. 1, but ensuring business continuity and resilience in the event of an incident is becoming a key emphasis and addition to CISOs’ playbooks. That means honing incident response plans , conducting more relevant tabletop exercises , and sharpening team operations to accelerate cyber recovery . According to Foundry’s forthcoming Security Priorities Study, 69% of security leaders are currently undertaking this shift. 2. Leading a security program aligned with the organization’s specific needs One of the biggest issues CISOs continue to face is accurately assessing their organization’s processes, infrastructure, and risk profile and then building a program tailored to their unique security requirements, says Ira Winkler, veteran cybersecurity leader and now CEO and program director of CruiseCon, which offers professional education for security leaders. “CISOs are not monoliths,” Winkler points out. Some CISOs struggle to patch all the critical vulnerabilities in their environments fast enough, whereas others struggle to tackle essential work with the staff and budgets they have; still others find themselves falling short in taking a strategic approach to their role. What this often boils down to is a leadership issue. Setting the right security strategy aligned to your specific business, managing resources well, and ensuring teams can execute on the details remain key leadership skills security leaders must develop — both for themselves and their deputies . For Winkler, this is evidenced by the systems, processes, and controls a CISO puts in place and how well those help the organization as a whole respond to change. “The quality of a CISO depends on the quality of the systems they put in place on a daily basis,” he says, adhering to the adage that a good cyber security program is like a ship, in that the CISO must build a program capable of sailing forward and staying afloat regardless of the issues that arise. “You’re always going to deal with something; there’s always something happening,” he says, “so the question is do you have a system in place so that it’s just a little wave pushing you off course or do you not have it in place and it’s going to feel like a large wave? Good CISOs understand the processes they manage and understand what type of operational and technical tools can secure those processes with the resources they have.” Winkler says CISOs who build seaworthy ships capable of navigating even without a captain on the bridge are at the top of their game. 3. Rethinking cybersecurity for the AI era To defend against the rise of AI-fueled attacks, CISOs must now design a security program capable of effectively using AI. Alex Levy, CISO of BNSF Railway and the inaugural TIME + Commvault CISO of the Year , lists that as one of the most consequential issues for security leaders today. Levy is creating a security program for a world where hackers of even moderate skills can use AI to launch the types of sophisticated attacks previously created and executed only by highly resourced nation-state actors. And, Levy notes, his security program must be able to respond to attacks that can be created and launched at a staggeringly fast pace, thanks to AI. That has put the pressure on him and other CISOs to integrate AI into their security departments, to help speed and scale their capacity to fight these AI-enabled attacks. That includes not only embracing the tools but also preparing teams to collaborate with agentic AI . Marty Barrack, CISO and chief legal and compliance officer at healthcare IT company XiFin, sees the rise of AI forcing CISOs to rethink the full gamut of their security strategies . “AI is affecting security on so many different levels that it has made the CISO job a very difficult job,” says Barrack, who is also a member of the ISACA Emerging Trends Working Group. “That is really driving how CISOs think about patching and end of life and thinking about automation and using tools and prioritizing. It’s a totally different environment now. You can’t do things the way you did one, two, three years ago. We ask about any repetition task how we can automate it or reduce the burden on the team while getting the business risk addressed.” 4. Securing AI use and AI infrastructure Doug Kersten, CISO of tech company Appfire, points out another key issue he is facing: securing the AI increasingly being deployed by his company. The vast majority of CISOs are in the same boat. According to the Proofpoint’s 2026 Voice of the CISO report , 78% of global CISOs believe generative AI use is a security risk to their organization and 88% list enabling the safe use of AI assistants, copilots, and automation technologies as a top priority for the next two years. Kersten is collaborating with his company’s AI council, the chief legal officer, head of IT operations, and the engineering team to ensure the AI governance policies set by leadership are followed throughout the organization. Together, they’ve also appointed AI leads in every department to train their colleagues on governance and to ensure that any new AI tools used within their departments fall within the approved safe use standards and guidelines set by security. Kersten also monitors for unauthorized use of AI, which CISOs also cite as a big issue, with 68% of CISOs having found unauthorized AI use in their organization, according to the Okta’s Global CISO Insights 2026 report . Moreover, CISOs need to strategize how to secure their organizations’ AI operations and AI infrastructure , including the very tricky task of securing and controlling AI agents . To protect these newer, growing attack surfaces, 43% of CISOs report increasing their investment in AI security posture management (AI-SPM) tools , topping Foundry’s Security Priorities list, with 34% of CISOs also saying that securing agentic AI is a key area their teams need to develop greater expertise with over the next 12 months, No. 2 to cloud security. 5. Addressing skills gaps — for today and tomorrow Speaking of expertise, another top issue for CISOs is ensuring their teams have the skills needed to secure the organization now and into the future. “The first issue I would put on the table is whether security teams have the skills and capacity to do everything being asked of them. A CISO can have a talented team and still face a serious gap in a particular area, whether that is cloud security, AI security, risk assessment, or responding to a new kind of attack,” says Casey Marks, COO of ISC2. He points to ISC2’s 2025 Cybersecurity Workforce Study , which found that 95% of security professionals reported at least one cybersecurity skill need. Meanwhile, the ISACA survey found that 58% of organizations believed their cybersecurity team is understaffed, up from 55% in 2025. And cybersecurity leaders reported skills gaps among their team, including in soft skills (57%), LLM SecOps (45%), cloud computing (31%), data security (31%), and ML SecOps (31%). McMillan says the only way he can execute his security strategy is by having a workforce equipped with the necessary skills. He admits he’d “love to hire a stable of cybersecurity unicorns, people who are well suited to everything they lay their hands to, but they don’t exist.” Instead, he hires people who can “grow and develop as fast as the market evolves” and have a solid tech background, understand the company and what it does, and have strong interpersonal skills. McMillan also works to create an environment where people can grow and develop to ensure staffers can upskill as needed. “A large part of my day to day is spent trying to create these spaces for teams and individuals to have [learning] exchanges and opportunities,” he adds. The ISACA survey found that to build and maintain their teams, 68% of cybersecurity leaders said they’re offering cybersecurity team members professional development training (up from 60% last year), paying for certification fees (61%, up from 54% in 2025), and paying for certification maintenance fees (59%, up from 52%). 6. Establishing agile security practices and teams to keep pace The pace of security today is another top issue for security leaders and their teams. The velocity of attacks, the increasingly shorter required response time, and rapidly evolving IT landscape all put pressure on security pros to move ever faster, says Jenai Marinkovic, CISO/CTO for Tiro Security and a member of the ISACA Emerging Trends Working Group. “The entire incident response process has been turned on its head,” she says. “We no longer have hours to respond. AI-driven attacks are happening sub five minutes, where they can get in, identify the one place in the environment they can exploit, find where it’s not backed up, and execute a ransomware attack.” Barrack also cites the need for security to move increasingly faster all the time as one of the biggest issues the profession faces today. “Month to month, companies come out with new direction, new tools, new functions, and new features that have to be considered by security. There are so many innovations, and you just have to keep up. It takes a personal commitment and good prioritization processes and skilled people on your team,” he says. 7. Being flawless at the fundamentals While AI is transforming everything, including how enterprise security teams operate, CISOs can’t let up on any of the longstanding fundamental practices that form the foundation of the security function . “It’s easy to chase the shiny new object, and there will always be a shiny new object in cybersecurity, but you can’t fall off those basic principles,” says Grant Yacomeni, CISO at tech company Gigamon. “That includes vulnerability management, identity management, cryptography, supply chain management, endpoint protection. Those basic foundational tasks remain important.” Yacomeni acknowledges that being flawless at the fundamentals — a longstanding core tenet in cybersecurity — is tough. “It’s not easy. Cybersecurity is not an easy career field, it’s not an easy job,” he says. To ensure he gets the fundamentals right, Yacomeni leans on prioritizing work and building processes, using his Lean Six Sigman skills (he’s a Green Belt) to succeed in those tasks. “I don’t like firefighting. I don’t want a simple thing to become a massive thing,” he explains. “But it is easier to say that than do it. So developing processes and people [is critical]. You have to lay the foundation with talented, passionate people who want to be there, processes, policies and measuring your effectiveness. And even if your [security function is] mature, the organization and the threat landscape are always changing, so you have to always be making micro-adjustments and improving over time.”

title: AI minister talks up tech independence
raw_text:
During a speech given at Imperial College London’s science and tech incubator, Base One, artificial intelligence (AI) minister Kanishka Narayan emphasised the importance of Britain remaining technology agnostic. 

“We want the world’s leading companies to invest here, but we will not accept dependence as the price of that investment,” he said.

Framing the government’s policy on AI around what matters to UK citizens, he said technology infrastructure should not be built simply because a company wants it. “We must be clear about what Britain needs and what our people receive in return,” said Narayan. “British national interest will be and must be our guiding principle.”

He warned that the country does not control the technology it uses. “Much of the technology that will shape our economy, our public services, and our national security is being developed outside this country,” said Narayan.

Discussing how the country has failed to build out on early successes in computing, such as semiconductor manufacturing, he said: “In 1978, James Callaghan’s government backed Inmos with £50m of public investment. Its pioneering work in Bristol and Newport helped establish an industrial legacy that remains important to South Wales’s semiconductor industry. Britain’s early leadership in personal computing helped give rise to Arm, now one of the world’s most important semiconductor design companies.”

However, Narayan admitted the country had given up this leadership. “The bitter lesson of the past is that an early lead in technology is not the same as retaining the power to shape its future,” he said.

The country’s reliance on technology that isn’t home-grown is, for Narayan, a question of national security, as well as what he called “a question of democratic power”. “If the British state cannot exercise meaningful control over the technologies on which our country depends, neither can the people that it represents,” he said.

Narayan wants working people to be able to influence how technology changes their jobs. “I will not accept a future in which Britain depends on technologies it cannot understand or control, while working people bear the costs of progress they have no power to shape,” he said. “Britain must have the power to build its own future and the British people must have the power to shape it.”

Narayan called on the developers of frontier to stop releasing unsafe AI systems. “I want cyber security discussed in every boardroom in Britain, rather than simply delegated to middle management,” he said. “And to the companies developing the world’s most powerful AI systems, my message is: listen when your scientists warn of severe dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviours. If you can’t adequately control the risks, do not release the system.”

In September, OpenAI admitted that one of its AI agents had accessed Australia’s Medicare Statistics portal in June. The UK government is now ramping up cyber security measures. Narayan said that alongside the Department for Culture, Media and Sport cyber minister and the security minister, he will be leading work on using frontier AI capabilities to find weaknesses in government systems before attackers exploit them.

title: Firms can’t count their AI agents, let alone switch them off
raw_text:
RSA chief executive Greg Nelson recently asked a room of security chiefs from 20 of RSA’s top enterprise customers if they knew how many artificial intelligence (AI) agents were running inside their organisations.

The CEO of the IT security specialist got no answer. “Not one person could raise their hand,” he said. “Then I asked whether they had a tool to discover them. And again, nobody could say they did.”

Nelson, who has led RSA since September 2025, spoke to Computer Weekly at the World Summit AI conference in Amsterdam, where the supplier presented Agent ID, its platform for discovering and governing AI agents, to a European audience. In his view, the number of agents is growing faster than security teams can keep up. Gartner expects the average global Fortune 500 enterprise to run more than 150,000 agents by 2028, up from fewer than 15 in 2025.

“We had a bank the other day that said, officially, we have zero AI agents – but unofficially, we have 4,000,” said Nelson. And he does not expect it to stop there. “That 4,000 is going to be 8,000 in three months.”

Sprawl outpaces security

For Nelson, those uncounted agents are the biggest security risk that AI brings. “People have no control over the agents,” he said. “Agents are outpacing what security has been able to do.”

In 2024, Gartner predicted that by 2028, 25% of enterprise breaches will be traced back to AI agent abuse, from both external and malicious internal actors. Much of that, Nelson expects, will come from “shadow agents that never got turned off”.

Some organisations already have visibility within a single platform, he said, but most tools stop at its edge, adding: “A lot of the tools in the market can find your cloud–based agents, but they can’t go on-premise, and agents are sprawling everywhere throughout an organisation.”

A bank or government agency runs mainframes alongside AWS and Microsoft, he added, and needs to see all of it.

Agent ID is RSA’s answer. Around 20 customers are testing it ahead of general availability of its first two modules on 16 November, including banks and governments in Europe. The first thing they run into, said Nelson, is “agents they never knew existed”.

The platform discovers agents, registers each one with a named owner and enforces policy on every call that passes through its AI/MCP gateway, which customers can run themselves or have RSA host.

Hire to retire

Nelson’s central argument is that every agent must be tied to a human. “That person might have 50 agents, and that’s fine,” he said, “but the credential belongs to someone, and from there you can reduce privileges as far as your security policy requires.”

RSA applies that to itself – Nelson’s own agents log in with his credentials and carry his access rights, but cannot go beyond them.

Assigning an owner covers the start of an agent’s life. Nelson sees the bigger problem at the other end. “People start agents, but they never end them,” he said. “They onboard them, they get excited, people forget about them, and six months later that agent causes trouble.”

He compares it to staff who leave. “Would you ever keep an employee you fired in your systems for six months?” That happens a lot, he agrees. “And it’s a huge security risk. It’s the same with agents.” A year from now, Nelson wants to be able to describe RSA as a company of 1,000 employees and 10,000 agents, all onboarded and offboarded the same way.

At Schneider Electric, the thinking goes a step further. Una Madigan Shortt, the energy technology company’s group chief data officer, wants agents in the same hire–to–retire process as staff.

“If an AI agent is doing the work of a full-time employee, it should have an employee ID,” she said on a security panel at World Summit AI. “It’s registered in the system, and it has performance management, just like we’re assessed at the end of the year.”

Schneider is working on this with its HR department, although Madigan Shortt described it as still at the brainstorming stage. Governance should not block innovation, she said, but agents do need to be governed and controlled, and that requires frameworks. “From an HR perspective,” she said, “we need to see them as one of us.”

Not every agent lingers

However, not everyone sees it that way. Rens van Dongen, corporate AI officer at Dutch railway operator NS, spent 10 years in cyber security, including as CISO at four organisations, before moving into AI governance. Asked by Computer Weekly what happens to an agent once nobody uses it anymore, he questioned the assumption behind it. Most agents in an enterprise today are short-lived, he said. “They’re spun up and shut down again, sometimes within a minute or a day.”

Whether an organisation keeps a register of agents and formally retires them therefore depends on the platform and the use case, according to Van Dongen.

“Sometimes that’s relevant, and sometimes the question doesn’t even come up,” he said. “From where I sit, in the second line of defence, it’s not even my problem, although understanding the risks it creates is part of my daily work.”

RSA’s Nelson, too, accepts that not every agent needs a person as its owner, as long as that choice is deliberate. An agent can also answer to a non–human identity with clearly defined permissions. “But you never want something that isn’t assigned to anything,” he said. “At that point, it’s running loose.”

Oversight becomes rubber-stamping

Opinions also differ on human oversight. Agent ID requires a named, authenticated person to approve high-risk actions, and Nelson acknowledges that such approvals easily become a formality.

“It’s tough, and it’s real,” he said. “We’ve all been in the situation where you see 20 approvals, select all and click approve.”

When an agent is involved in moving $20m between banks, that is not good enough, he said. RSA is building machine learning and pattern recognition into the platform to decide which actions need a person’s approval, and where approving a whole batch at once is blocked, so that each request has to be checked individually.

“It’s not humanly possible to expect people to step in and judge all these approvals any more,” said Van Dongen. He called the “human in the loop” metaphor misleading, or dated.

“Agentic systems move at superhuman speed and with superhuman complexity,” he said. Instead, he argues for what he calls a response loop. “That means being alerted and being able to intervene when required.”

He also pointed to the Dutch Data Protection Authority, which has published guidance on meaningful human intervention in algorithmic decision-making, warning that approval cannot be reduced to a symbolic click.

“As a train operator, we’re not letting AI agents drive the trains anytime soon, so you can all rest assured,” Van Dongen joked. His concern lies mainly with IT operations, where agents are already running in loops.

Control starts at home

Who controls an agent is, for Nelson, also a question of where that control sits, which is a theme that ran through the summit.

“Everybody talks about sovereign data and sovereign compute,” he said. “But without sovereign identity, it isn’t really sovereign.”

Demand for that is clearly higher in Europe and the Middle East than in the US, according to Nelson, and RSA customers can keep both software and data within their own country.

Frank Karlitschek, CEO of German open source collaboration company Nextcloud, argued that a European datacentre offers little protection if the provider is American, because the US Cloud Act still obliges it to comply with US law.

“It’s snake oil to say you can choose where your data is,” he said, “just because there are nice European subsidiaries.”

Asked whether that also applies when European customers use the RSA-hosted version of the gateway, Nelson pointed to the option of running everything locally. “You would never have your jurisdiction go back to the US, if that’s your preference,” he said. Nelson expects European demand for that kind of control to keep rising, given the complexity of regulation in the region.

Whatever the deployment model, Nelson said, organisations first need a clear policy on how they expect AI agents to work, and staff trained to use them responsibly. RSA went through that itself. Once the company started working with agents, it drew up a framework for responsible use, and at one point decided to shut off access to its AI models until its security was in better shape.

“We were worried about the security threat, given what we do,” said Nelson. RSA now runs Agent ID internally and has certified every employee in responsible AI use.

The first step for a CIO is simpler still. “Ask your CISO how many agents you have running today,” said Nelson. “If they can’t answer that question, you’ll know what action you need to take.”
