title: Enterprises are growing the use of AI – but proving what it earns is the harder part
raw_text:
A year ago, Hiek van der Scheer measured the progress of his company’s artificial intelligence (AI) projects by the number of use cases. As chief data and AI officer at Dutch bank ABN Amro, he had a target for the number of AI applications the organisation managed to get into production. The business case behind each one mattered, but not that much. Today, that’s changed.

“Now, every use case we take live has a business case,” he said, speaking at the World Summit AI conference in Amsterdam earlier in October. To get funding, an AI project has to show results in at least one of five measures the bank has set – lower costs, growth, higher customer satisfaction, better use of capital or reduced risk.

Marco Bressan, chief scientist at the Spain’s Banco Santander, has seen what happens when nobody asks for the business case. Companies hand out AI assistants and copilots, and “people do get more productive”, he said, “but they end up doing other things, or generating work for others. So, it’s very hard to justify that productivity, and all those tokens flying out of the window.” He has a name for it – the adoption trap.

Most organisations, Bressan said, promise to save so many hours: “But it’s not precise. It’s not in the books.” His bank’s way out is to move as quickly as possible from tools to AI products, such as mortgages and consumer finance offerings that use AI, where the value can be captured and shown.

Santander has committed to generating more than €1bn in business value from AI between 2026 and 2028, through extra revenue and lower costs. In the first quarter of this year, the bank reported €35m, and it expects more than €200m by year-end.

Axa has made a similar promise to its investors. Giovanni D’Aniello, group CIO of the French insurer, said Axa has been getting value from AI for more than a decade. In its Growing forward strategic plan, presented in September, the group put a figure on the next phase – €500m to €700m in annual recurring pre-tax benefits from scaling AI by 2029.

For many other organisations, such numbers are still some way off. At ING Belgium, AI now pulls company information from the Belgian Official Gazette, where firms publish changes such as new directors, and updates the bank’s systems automatically, work that used to be done by hand.

“It frees up time for other things,” said Bram Joostens, customer journey expert in business lending at ING Belgium, told Computer Weekly. “But we’ve only just rolled it out, so it’s hard to say anything concrete yet.”

Meanwhile, the next step is being built at the bank – an agent that checks incoming business loan applications for missing documents.

Forcing the numbers

What separates the organisations that can put a figure on AI from those that can’t is often who forces the question. At ABN Amro, it comes from the top. Van der Scheer doesn’t pretend measuring is easy though.

“Because the whole environment is changing, it’s sometimes hard to pinpoint whether something is really down to AI or to something else we’re doing,” he said. Even so, he works with the bank’s controllers to measure every use case against the five key metrics.

At AMD, it was cost that forced the question. When the chipmaker started deploying agents across the company, “the AI token bill took off astronomically,” chief technology officer Mark Papermaster told Computer Weekly.

His chief financial officer responded with a condition. “Look, we’ll spend the money,” Papermaster recalled her saying, “as long as we’re sure we’re getting the return on the investment.” Every group that applies AI now budgets for it in the normal budgeting process and owns proving the benefit.

Others measure application by application. “A/B testing is how medical companies have measured whether a drug works for a very long time,” said Pierre-Yves Calloc’h, former chief digital officer at French drinks group Pernod Ricard, where he spent six years deploying AI at scale.

One of those deployments gave sales reps in more than 28 countries a recommendation every Monday morning on which stores and bars to visit, and what to do once there. By comparing reps who got the recommendations with reps who didn’t, the drinks group could attribute a few million euros in benefit to it.

Pratyus Sinha, until recently senior director of responsible AI at Decathlon, starts measuring even earlier – before anything is built. When he was asked to overhaul the AI behind the sports retailer’s e-commerce platform, there were already hundreds of possible use cases on the table.

“You could just put a finger in the air and say, this one’s worth a hundred million,” he said. “But when you look at the assumptions behind that number, it quickly falls apart.” So, his team built a framework to choose between them, weighing revenue potential, risk and capacity, but above all how measurable each use case was.

Website search passed that test because its value can be calculated – missed queries multiplied by the conversion rate and the average basket value. Even so, a calculation was not enough, said Sinha. The new search agent was first tested in production with real customers, through A/B tests and a gradual roll-out, and only then scaled up.

Proof before code

Retailer Albert Heijn, a market leader among Dutch supermarkets, takes that caution further still. “We’d actually rather not use AI,” said Noortje van Genugten, the company’s vice-president of product. “If we can solve a problem more easily another way, we will.”

Its stores employ many teenagers in their first job, who are regularly asked by customers about products they have never heard of. The team suspected AI could help but wasn’t sure enough to invest. So, they added an assistant to the retailer’s in-house staff app, but initially without any AI behind it.

“My team sat in the back room of the store and answered every question themselves,” Van Genugten said. “Because we wanted to understand which questions were being asked before building anything. Maybe AI wasn’t the solution.”

Most questions turned out to be about range, stock, location in the store, price and promotions. Only then did the team build the real assistant, which still answers just that one kind of question. Albert Heijn has 125,000 staff, and the assistant now handles around 80,000 conversations a week.

Process before AI

For much of his talk, the screens beside Santander’s Bressan showed The Flintstones, the cartoon family whose stone-age life was a copy of 1960s suburbia, down to the toaster.

“Many corporations are like the writers of The Flintstones,” he said. “They want exactly the same operating model they have today, only with AI.” Many processes were designed for people to hand work to one another, he argued, and translating them one-to-one for AI misses what the technology can do.

D’Aniello sees the same reflex in insurance. Even Axa’s most modern core applications, he said, are essentially digitised versions of old paper-based processes, down to the order of the tasks and the data each step requires.

“If you’ve been an underwriter or a claims handler for 25 years, your natural behaviour when redesigning a process for agents is to replicate what you know,” he said. “But that doesn’t really work, because agentic transformation is not about automation.”

Automation, in his view, is the smallest part of the value. His first advice to staff is to forget the past and start with a blank page.

Papermaster offered AMD’s chip design process as evidence. Before agentic AI, the company found dozens of places where AI improved individual tasks. “We got 1%, 3%, 5% productivity gains,” he said. “Very helpful – but it didn’t significantly shorten the time it takes us to get new chips to market.”

That changed when models became capable enough to chain those tasks together – one agent with perhaps 10 specialised sub-agents underneath it, much like a team of experts. Applied to the whole design workflow, he said, that is now saving months on an effort that typically takes 18 months to two years and has allowed AMD to keep growing without expanding its workforce at the rate it once did.

At Pernod Ricard, the recommendations only paid off if sales reps followed them – with 10% adoption, the company would get 10% of the value. It aimed for 85%, and got there by making the job more interesting, freeing reps from spreadsheets to do the store visits and personal contact they enjoyed.

“The technology is complex, but it’s not the most complex part,” Calloc’h said.

AMD came to the same conclusion. The biggest change it needed was in culture and mindset, and every employee now has to complete AI training, while an agentic AI centre of excellence supports the rest of the company. Success stories are shared internally, and “when engineers see what another group achieved, that spurs them on”, Papermaster said.

D’Aniello made a related point about Axa: “If you don’t give all your employees access to these tools, it’s very difficult for them to imagine completely different workflows.”

Calloc’h is also candid about what he missed. His Monday morning recommendations for sales reps served a large population making many small decisions – but the biggest decisions, such as which brands to invest in or how to divide millions between countries, were still taken in the boardroom with Excel and PowerPoint. “And it’s still the case today in most companies I’ve been talking to,” he said.

An owner for every agent

As agents take on more work, the speakers kept returning to who answers for what they do.

“Even before AI, if you were accountable, you had to test the work and stand behind it,” said Papermaster. “That doesn’t change with AI.” At AMD, every agent has a manager.

Van der Scheer said of ABN Amro’s mortgage process that “we will never say: the computer says no”, with a human always taking the final decision. To keep agents in check, the bank splits them into layers. A conversational agent talks to customers or staff, a reasoning agent checks every request against the bank’s policies before passing it on, and task agents carry out the work.

That middle layer exists because an agent always wants to please, he explained – with the right questions, a conversational agent can be talked past its limits.

Axa, which operates in 52 countries, has centralised the gatekeeping. Its minimum set of guardrails was designed together with a handful of leading countries and built into modules of Axa’s agentic hub.

“Countries can do more,” D’Aniello said, “but they cannot do less.” Any business unit or claims manager that wants to start using agents has to go through central teams, which check what can be reused and make sure those guardrails are in place.

Not everyone on stage drew the line in the same place. Sinha argued that people should be able to stop an agent but not steer it, and that within clear boundaries and with a limited blast radius, it should act fully autonomously. The manager stays accountable, he said, but the action itself should not wait for a human.

Axa keeps a human both in and on the loop of every process, and D’Aniello draws a sharp line between the two. “In the loop” means deliberately leaving a share of the work with people. “What you want to avoid is that, over time, the real expertise of Axa sits in the agentic ecosystem,” he said, “and not in the heads of our specialists anymore.”

“On the loop” means experts who watch in real time how agents handle a claim, with the power to stop it, and who review afterwards what was done.

Van der Scheer sees it going the other way. ABN Amro uses agents across its software development lifecycle, with a human checking every step. But if the code is 95% right, he said, the reviewer only finds the remaining 5%, and that soon stops being an effective control.

He is convinced that within a few years nobody will review code by hand anymore, while the bank will still need to control it. “You can say there was human oversight,” he said, “but if it’s just a stamping machine, you don’t have effective control. On what human oversight really means, the jury is still out.”

title: The Security Interviews: A post-Mythos reality check
raw_text:
Human beings are no longer the only users of enterprise IT systems. Artificial intelligence (AI) is accelerating machine-to-machine communications, with intelligent agents working on behalf of humans to complete tasks. Often, these agents will need to touch enterprise IT systems and internal and external websites to achieve their objective.

Enterprise IT security professionals need to reassess their cyber security strategy in light of the advances in agentic AI and, in particular, the effectiveness of frontier AI models to break into IT systems.

When Anthropic’s Claude Mythos AI model was unveiled on 7 April 2026, it changed the threat landscape, collapsing the window between discovery and weaponisation.

Earlier this year, Amazon Web Services (AWS) introduced Continuum, a cyber security tool that it positions as a defence against AI-powered cyber attacks.

The hyperscaler developed Continuum because it believes the way enterprise IT security has been done in the past – collecting and storing telemetry to be queried and presented on dashboards – cannot keep pace with AI-accelerated cyber attacks. Continuum aims to address the new risks posed by AI-powered attacks by automating vulnerability scans and prioritising patching.

According to AWS, Continuum for code vulnerabilities addresses the full lifecycle of a code vulnerability at what it calls “machine speed” from discovery through actions. Continuum is model agnostic, using multiple frontier models to reason over an IT environment.

The future of IT security

Rudra Mitra, vice-president of security services at AWS, was recently in the UK for the AWS London Summit, which focused on financial services. One of the areas discussed at the event was the future of IT security. “I think the topic du jour is very much not just AI, but the speed at which security attacks are now moving,” he says.

Speaking on the Computer Weekly Downtime Upload podcast, Mitra says cyber security is now in the “post-Mythos era”. Anthropic’s Mythos model demonstrated how effective a frontier model can be at attacking IT systems, which means finding and weaponising vulnerabilities can be achieved at an accelerated rate due to advances in AI.

• Listen to the full interview with AWS’s Rudra Mitra here •

“In the ‘post-Mythos’ world, the time to find and weaponise vulnerabilities has accelerated dramatically. It’s incredible how, with these frontier AI models, it’s getting supercharged. You can find vulnerabilities that scale much faster, and it’s much cheaper,” he says.

From an enterprise IT security perspective, he says: “We’ve got to have a response for security that also moves at machine speed, which is not the way IT security was done before.”

A best practice in cyber security is the multilayered approach to enterprise IT security, which is built on top of industry collaboration and responsible disclosure. Here, the time from when a security hole is discovered to when it is made public is controlled to enable patches and workarounds to be developed and tested.

No such luxury exists when there is a zero-day attack, but cyber security teams are well-versed in handling such situations. However, advanced AI-powered attacks rewrite the rulebook since IT security operations teams now need to address cyber security threats at what Mitra calls “machine speed”.

Defending at machine speed

The idea of cyber security tools to enable IT security operations to run at “machine speed” has implications for IT security teams and ethical hacking. If an AI can scan the attack surface and spot security holes far quicker than a human, what role does the cyber security specialist play in enterprise IT security operations? Mitra says: “I think security today looks like it’s human centred with AI assisting.”

This, he says, is the state of the art and implies that the speed of a response to a cyber threat is very much governed by humans, where the IT security operations team still relies on monitoring security dashboards. The IT security team assesses the risk and takes appropriate action.

“We’ve got to have a response for security that also moves at machine speed, which is not the way IT security was done before”

Rudra Mitra, AWS

In Mitra’s view, enterprise IT security needs to move forward with machine-speed security overlaid with human judgement. This is something he believes may require a rethink of how organisations tackle cyber security. AI, he says, should not simply be bolted onto existing IT security operations.

“I wonder if we should be thinking about redesigning security completely for machines,” he adds.

Mitra believes that to tackle cyber security threats that may well be agentic in nature, cyber security teams need agentic AI tools. “If you think about security systems like Continuum, where we’re redesigning for a world which is more agentic, the systems for security have to be agentic,” he says.

Mitra recognises the value of using AI in monitoring cyber security. But he also sees a role for people, where there is a human in the loop to provide a level of judgement. “This becomes the ‘super interesting’ job in security going forward,” he says. 

Offloading mundane tasks to AI

If IT security professionals are spending much of their time fire-fighting security breaches, assessing false positives and applying patches, they have little time left to tackle more complex problems.

With agentic AI doing much of that work, Mitra hopes “95% of the mundane work can be offloaded”, giving the IT security professional more time to focus on what Mitra sees as the more exciting part of the job, which is the judgement role.

It is likely that much of what falls into the domain of ethical hacking today will be replaced by AI-based systems, like Continuum, which are able to identify vulnerabilities in code autonomously. “As security professionals, we spend so much time on the noise. It’s very important for us to think about how the security professional is able to engage in higher-value tasks,” Mitra adds.

Looking at how enterprise systems are evolving, it is pretty clear that agentic AI is the direction of travel for the tech sector. The end user of an IT system may or may not be a real person – it could be an AI agent working on behalf of a human user to automate a series of tasks. This makes it much harder to determine if the calls to an application programming interface (API), or clicks through on an application or website, represent a real user, an AI working for a real user or an AI-powered cyber attack.

Mitra believes observability becomes increasingly important for cyber defence. This requires an understanding of what actions are being taken deep within enterprise IT systems and represents a rich area of cyber security investment and industry collaboration.

In Mitra’s words, “security is a team sport” and “it’s going to require many solution providers to work together”.

title: Quantum firms receive a £50m boost
raw_text:
The UK government has announced £50m funding for quantum technology firms to test and develop innovative products as part of its goal to invest £2bn in the technology.

Through a Sensing and Positioning, Navigation and Timing competition run by UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), the funding aims to support the development of quantum-based technology that has the potential to outperform existing technologies.

While quantum technology is not widely available commercially, it is something the government sees as a big opportunity for the UK. Quantum computers promise to tackle difficult computational problems that cannot be solved using traditional supercomputer architectures. There is also growing interest in quantum sensing and quantum security.

In March, the Labour government, under Keir Starmer’s premiership, announced it would invest £1bn over the next four years to enable the UK to win the race to deliver quantum computing at scale. This was followed by further funding commitments in the government’s industrial strategy. As part of a £670m package of funding to accelerate the UK’s quantum computing capabilities, Labour announced 10-year funding for the National Quantum Computing Centre.

One of the projects to win UKRI funding is a quantum monitoring system led by West Midlands-based MoniRail. The technology being developed could be used to pinpoint the precise location of faults in railway tracks and signalling equipment, where GPS is unable to reach.

Another winning project is a handheld quantum eye developed by Bristol-based Siloton, which aims to make advanced eye diagnostics available outside specialist hospitals.

Also receiving backing is Oxfordshire-based Coldquanta UK, which is developing a compact, mobile quantum radio system that can locate signals with high accuracy. Application areas include operational intelligence in the military, improving resilience of critical infrastructure such as airports, and helping emergency responders locate distress signals.

Other companies to be funded include QLM Technology, which is developing a camera to see and measure greenhouse gases in energy; Quantum Fabrix, a developer of a next-generation clock for satellites; and Cerca Magnetics, which is developing a wearable brain scanner.

Science, innovation and investment minister Chris McDonald said: “We’re backing teams across the UK to turn bright ideas into products that make a real difference, growing the economy, creating new jobs and ensuring we can be leaders in quantum technology for decades to come.”

Charlotte Deane, executive chair of the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council at UK Research and Innovation, said: “This UKRI funding gives these businesses what they need to grow and take their technology further, while building strong UK supply chains that keep the parts quantum tech depends on here in the UK. 

“These technologies also matter for our national security, giving our military and emergency responders reliable ways to navigate and stay connected even when conventional systems can’t be relied on.”

Along with the Sensing and Positioning, Navigation and Timing competition, Innovate UK, the UK’s national innovation agency, which is part of UKRI, is funding the development of quantum communications. Through its Enabling Commercial Quantum Networking competition, Innovate UK is investing £20m in UK-based businesses to build domestic capability in quantum communication networks.

UKRI also announced an £8m expansion of its Quantum Enabling Skills Training (QuEST) apprentices programme to create new routes into skilled quantum jobs.

title: Campaign group submits evidence to two Capita probes as pension scheme member turns to food bank
raw_text:
A group set up to support civil service pension scheme (CSPS) members in difficulty has written to MPs and the National Audit Office (NAO) to offer support in ongoing investigations into Capita’s botched scheme administration.

Delays in paying pensions has forced at least one former civil servant to use a food bank as many struggle financially.

In a letter to MPs on the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) and the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee (Pacac), the Civil Service Pensions Campaign group described Capita’s “systemic” failure.

The group, which represents thousands of retired civil servants, has also requested that the NAO take direct contributions to its current investigation from group members, who are all members of the CSPS.

Capita had a two-year period to prepare for the takeover of the administration of 1.7 million civil servant pensions, but since taking the wheel in December 2025, it has overseen a disaster.

Retiring civil servants have seen long delays in being paid their pensions, with some still not in receipt of them despite retiring 10 months ago.

About 4,000 emergency loans have been made to struggling members of the scheme, and people have died before receiving what they are owed.

MPs listening

In a submission to MPs on the PAC and the Pacac, the campaign group wrote: “This is a systemic failure. The evidence being reported to the Campaigns Group suggests that these problems can no longer reasonably be characterised as a collection of isolated administrative errors or particularly difficult individual cases.”

The campaign group told Computer Weekly: “Various Facebook groups dedicated to sharing [CSPS] experiences reveal the anguish and anger of claimants forced to rely on food banks, reliant on the financial charity of friends and family, and the sadness of postponed retirement plans.

“Some claimants have died whilst waiting for payment and bereaved relatives have endured months of contradictory guidance on claiming pensions,” it said. “Others have spent hours every week trying to obtain information from Capita call handlers who don’t appear to have access to the right IT systems and fob off callers with empty claims to “escalate issues”. 

“Members report problems across virtually every part of the service,” it added.

The campaign group said these include longstanding unresolved cases, delayed retirement quotations, delayed pension payments, unresolved bereavement cases and problems with ill-health retirement.

Members have also complained of unanswered correspondence, unanswered portal messages, inaccurate and incomplete information, repeated telephone calls producing little progress, ineffective escalation, and limited information available to telephone agents.

The group added that MPs are struggling to get “meaningful answers”. “These are not simply administrative delays,” it said. “They have real financial and human consequences.”

One pension scheme member recently said they have been forced to use a food bank and take their car off the road.

Watchdog on the case

The NAO announced last week that it will investigate the status of the scheme, transition arrangements at go-live, how Capita has performed, and the impact on member experience. It will also investigate how the Cabinet Office has exercised its responsibilities for oversight of the scheme.

The group has written to the government spending watchdog requesting details of how it can contribute. “We ask the NAO to recognise the Campaigns Group as a stakeholder contributing direct member evidence and to agree a consultation process while the investigation is underway,” it said.

title: AI: Faster than the speed of safety
raw_text:
Microsoft president Brad Smith has called on governments and artificial intelligence (AI) firms to work together to implement safety in AI systems. He believes the pace of AI development is moving forward faster than the ability of AI safety to keep up.

Speaking on the BBC’s Today programme, Smith said: “Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI. Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection. We know how to do this for other products. We should build on that knowledge and start to think about how to apply it to AI.” 

He urged AI firms to build on knowledge of safety and apply this to AI systems. “You often get your best work done, especially on something like a safety break, for example, when the industry itself starts to develop common standards,” Smith told the Today programme.

He said this requires identifying best practices and developing standards, which regulators can adopt to put in place a legal obligation for compliance. 

For Smith, the UK is well placed to advance AI safety standards thanks to the AI Safety Institute. “I actually think the country and the government that is in the best position to advance AI safety standards and even rules is the United Kingdom and the AI Security Institute,” he said. “You need capability to do this well and you need to have trained people.”

Smith’s comments on the UK’s AI safety readiness preceded the UK government’s announcement to strengthen government cyber defences. Speaking at Imperial College London’s science and tech incubator, Base One, AI minister Kanishka Narayan argued for a whole-society approach to resilience in the face of emerging AI risks, so that this technology continues to serve British people’s interests and boost our prosperity, as well as our security.

He warned that as frontier AI systems become increasingly powerful and capable of acting autonomously, the potential consequences of failures or malicious use could become far more serious. Narayan argued that Britain needs to act now to strengthen its defences and prepare for future serious incidents. “I want Britain to become one of the hardest countries in the world to attack using artificial intelligence,” he said.

“We will legislate wherever necessary,” he said. “And we won’t look to law alone. We will look to British ingenuity: our scientific expertise, technological capabilities and institutions to understand these increasingly powerful systems.”

The government also sees the emerging field of AI verification as an important part of efforts to reduce serious AI risk.

title: Undercover agent: Can process mining police AI automation?
raw_text:
“The challenge is monumental. Even under the best circumstances, the transition to this new AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history,” wrote Bill Gates in an essay last month. It’s the sort of hyperbolic artificial intelligence (AI) warning to which we are growing accustomed, fuelled as much by corporate reaction to AI as the technology itself.

According to Gartner, businesses are turning to AI agents in droves with the promise of doing more with less. Around 80% of large organisations piloting or deploying AI agents, intelligent automation and other autonomous technologies have already reduced their workforce. But do these organisations really think that cutting people out of processes translates into better returns?

Gartner’s answer appears to be no. Its research found little correlation between workforce reductions and improved returns from autonomous technologies. Cutting labour may reduce costs, but it does not necessarily make the underlying business work any better. The question, then, is whether organisations are using AI to rethink how work gets done, or simply inserting agents into processes built for people.

“A 12-step approvals chain built for a paper-based world stays a bad process after you shave 40 seconds off each step,” says Jason Strambi, manager, AI advisory at BearingPoint. It’s a good point, and perhaps where process mining is finding a new relevance.

Traditionally, process mining is used to monitor and analyse business processes. It uses event data from enterprise resource planning (ERP) and customer relationship management (CRM) applications, for example, to identify bottlenecks, abnormalities and inefficiencies. So, in many respects, it is a backwards-looking, reactive tool – but this is where AI is starting to change the possibilities and what this could mean to an organisation.

Rather than simply asking what happened to a process and why, organisations can increasingly use that understanding to anticipate what might happen next and provide AI systems with context about how work is supposed to get done.

That’s the theory, anyway.

“Process mining is undergoing a fundamental repositioning,” says Bernhard Schaffrik, principal analyst at Forrester, “from a retrospective analytics tool into becoming the operational infrastructure for agentic AI.”

But Schaffrik is quick to point out that this is by no means happening overnight.

“Technically viable; operationally nascent,” is how he describes the current state of autonomous AI acting on process intelligence. A Forrester survey of 15 process intelligence suppliers, he says, reveals “a clear execution gap”, with supplier messaging racing ahead of both product capability and customer adoption.

Demand from prospective customers to use process intelligence as a precursor to AI averaged 52%, according to the survey, compared with average adoption among existing customers of 34%. Only a third of suppliers reported broad customer use across agent observation, training and performance improvement.

Counter measures

While AI can make process mining more accessible and potentially more predictive, process mining can also provide AI with an understanding of how work actually gets done inside a particular organisation. Think of it as an extra pair of eyes, keeping watch on the comings and goings of work processes, reporting back in simpler terms, thanks to generative AI.

Rather than requiring specialist skills to interrogate event logs and build dashboards, users can increasingly ask questions in natural language. Michael Curry, president of data modernisation at Rocket Software, says AI can also take this further, enabling “predictions and simulation-based recommendations”, potentially moving process mining beyond identifying what went wrong towards anticipating problems before they occur.

Peter van der Putten, director of the AI Lab at Pegasystems and assistant professor of AI at Leiden University, sees a change in expectations. Businesses, he says, increasingly want AI that “drives action, not just insight”, bringing process mining much closer to the execution of the processes it was traditionally used to analyse.

Things become more interesting when the relationship is reversed. Instead of asking what AI can do for process mining, businesses are beginning to ask what process mining can do for AI. An agent given access to company data may be able to retrieve information or execute a task, but that does not necessarily mean it understands where that task sits within a wider business process, what should happen next, or the rules and dependencies that govern it.

Process intelligence potentially provides some of that missing operational context. The key word here is “potentially”.

Schaffrik sees three emerging roles for process intelligence here. The first is helping to train agents using operational process data. Then it can help design them by providing a structured picture of processes and their rules. And finally, it can observe what agents do once they are deployed. As organisations give agents greater freedom, this last point becomes particularly important.

Van der Putten points to another possibility. He says process mining can itself be applied to the execution trails left by AI agents, identifying recurring patterns that could then be converted into “simpler, more predictable and lower-cost workflows”.

In theory, this gives an agent more than access to the underlying data. Process information can provide context around the sequence in which work happens, the relationships between different activities and the rules that have historically governed them. Schaffrik says knowledge graphs built from process data can provide “the semantic grounding that limits agent hallucinations or agents acting outside organisational intent”.

That can only be a good thing, surely. Curry certainly sees the potential.

“I think this is the promise of process mining in the world of AI,” says Curry. “Autonomous monitoring and agentic remediation represent an exciting future state for process mining. This really changes the nature of process mining, and transforms it into process governance and remediation. However, this is still aspirational for most organisations.”

He also believes process mining can provide agents with something approaching a set of rails on which to operate.

“Process mining can now be used as ground truth to instruct agents on the right steps to take under specific circumstances, making those decisions deterministic rather than probabilistic,” adds Curry.

Black box

But there is an obvious complication. AI agents remain probabilistic systems, no matter how much context is wrapped around them.

“Agentic AI will never be fully reliable as per its design. It will always remain somewhat of a black box since it is probabilistic in nature,” says Schaffrik. “Many decision-makers have this in mind when deciding about giving AI full autonomy over company operations.”

Giving an agent process context is of limited value if that context itself is incomplete or unreliable. Schaffrik identifies data readiness as the first bottleneck, with process data often fragmented across legacy systems, inconsistently logged or simply incomplete.

As agents begin to operate across multiple systems, businesses need to know not only what an agent is doing, but what it is permitted to do and who is accountable when something goes wrong. Schaffrik says most enterprises still lack the infrastructure needed to “register agents, enforce least-privilege access, maintain audit trails, and manage agent identity across heterogeneous environments.”

There is also a danger that businesses focus on controlling the agent without questioning the process it has been asked to follow.

“Enterprises are inserting agents into legacy, human-paced workflows and then wondering why step-change value doesn’t materialise because agents layered onto old processes inherit old constraints,” says Schaffrik.

It is a problem recognised by BearingPoint’s Strambi, too. Automating a process does not necessarily improve it. The problem becomes greater as more technology is layered on top. Strambi warns that businesses may be creating systems whose individual components can be understood, but whose overall actions become more difficult to explain.

“A process map feeding a prediction model feeding an agent that takes action is three layers of inference stacked on top of each other,” says Strambi. “You can explain each layer on its own, but it’s harder to explain the chain, and the chain is often what your customer experiences.”

Strambi says organisations have to decide where a human sits in the whole structure at the point at which you build that structure.

“If you leave it to chance, you get an architecture that works until the day it does not, and nobody can tell you why,” says Strambi.

Agent energy

There are examples of companies trying to put some of these ideas into practice. German energy company Uniper has put an AI agent built using Microsoft Copilot Studio into production in its recruitment and hiring operation, combining its HR data with operational context from Celonis.

During testing, Uniper ran the same prompts with and without that additional process context. Asked to identify bottlenecks in recruitment, the agent working from raw HR data produced generic responses. With process context, it was able to identify specific problems, including 27 candidates who had remained on shortlists for more than 14 days.

“With Celonis as our context layer, we’re building AI solutions that aren’t just tools we experiment with, but assistants we trust,” says Robert Daamen, head of Process Intelligence CoE at Uniper.

Trust, however, does not mean autonomy. Strambi’s question about where the human sits in the structure is still ringing in the ears, but Daamen at least says that as far as Uniper is concerned, “humans will always be in the loop and decision-makers – agents will only support”.

Despite using AI agents within the hiring process, Uniper does not allow them to assess candidates or make decisions that affect them.

“Our HR AI agents do not analyse candidate profiles or decide actions that affect candidates,” says Daamen. “Instead, the agents focus on process guidance and process management by automating administrative tasks, such as providing hiring manager briefings and reminders via Microsoft Teams and managing job requisition overviews.”

The agents can also analyse position data, he says, including finding similar roles that are currently open or have been advertised previously.

Uniper therefore illustrates both the potential and the current limits of the model. Process intelligence can give an agent a richer understanding of what is happening within a business process, but that does not necessarily mean handing the process over to it. For now, at least, the agent is helping people make and execute decisions rather than replacing them.

Not every organisation will draw the line in the same place, of course. There are so many variables still, depending on legacy systems, data quality and the raison d’etre for an organisation to pursue automation in the first place.

For Strambi, however, responsibility does not become any less human as autonomy increases. “Accountability stays with the human who decided what the agent could do, and no vendor contract or model card changes that,” he says.

That makes deciding what an agent should not be allowed to do as important as deciding what it can do. For Strambi, organisations need to make those choices before deployment rather than discovering the limits of autonomy when something goes wrong.

“Design the human role before you deploy the agent,” he says. “Which decisions can it take alone, which need a person to confirm, which are off limits? Every organisation has a threshold beyond which removing human judgement stops saving money and starts costing trust, and you have to find yours on purpose.”

This perhaps brings process mining back to its original purpose. Its value has always come from making the workings of an organisation more visible. AI may allow it to predict, recommend and increasingly provide the context within which agents operate, but that same visibility could become even more important as those agents are given greater freedom.

In that sense, process mining may be as important for understanding what organisations should not automate as it is for enabling what they can.
